articles.title: Ruby Buying Guide: Comparing Red Color, Cut and Disclosure
articles.summary: A practical starting point for comparing ruby appearance, requesting useful evidence and keeping your shortlist organized.
articles.body:
Ruby shopping becomes easier when you separate what you enjoy looking at from what still needs verification. Start with your preferred shade of red, a comfortable spending limit and the jewellery design you have in mind. A clear brief is more useful than searching for an impressive label without knowing what it describes.

Understand the name Ruby is the red variety of corundum, the mineral species that also includes sapphire. Chromium contributes its red color. Those facts explain the gem family, but they do not establish the identity, treatment history or origin of an individual stone. Keep those questions attached to the specific item you are considering.

Build a visual shortlist Choose three candidates and request comparable face-up photographs, side views and a short video for each. Record what you like in ordinary language: a lively red, a pleasing outline or a balanced appearance. Include measurements in the same note so you can discuss the intended setting with a jeweller.

Ask focused questions Request the exact item number, treatment disclosure and any available independent laboratory report. If a seller uses a color trade name, ask how that description is being applied. Avoid allowing a memorable phrase to replace the documents or the visual comparison you wanted.

Make the final comparison Use one page for every candidate: appearance, measurements, identity evidence, treatment information, total cost and unanswered questions. Then revisit your original brief. A useful purchase decision is one you can explain clearly, with the stone you prefer and the information that supports choosing it.

articles.title: Sapphire Beyond Blue: A Guide to Choosing Your Color
articles.summary: Explore sapphire as a color choice and learn how to turn broad preferences into a manageable shortlist.
articles.body:
Blue may be the first color you associate with sapphire, but it is only the beginning of the conversation. Before comparing individual stones, decide whether you want a familiar blue, a softer pink or another color direction. Keeping that preference visible will help you ask better questions and avoid collecting unrelated options.

Know the gem family Sapphire belongs to corundum. The name is used for corundum in colors other than the red associated with ruby. A listing's color name describes only part of the item; it is not a substitute for identifying the stone or disclosing its treatment history.

Compare a small selection Ask for a few candidates in your chosen color family rather than every available sapphire. Request consistent photographs and note which appearance you prefer before studying the descriptions. Write down whether you want a bold centerpiece, a quieter everyday design or a pair for earrings.

Prepare a setting brief Give your jeweller the actual length, width and depth of each shortlisted stone. Include the preferred metal, the overall style and any existing piece it should complement. If you are planning a pair, ask to compare both stones together rather than relying on separate photographs.

Keep the evidence with the item Save the seller's item reference, treatment statement, report details and quotation in one place. Ask for clarification when any of those records refer to a different stone. Your goal is a clear connection between the sapphire you selected, its description and the information supplied with it—not simply a beautiful photograph.

articles.title: Emerald Shopping: Looking Beyond a Beautiful Green Photograph
articles.summary: Organize an emerald comparison around appearance, item-specific information and the questions to ask before setting it.
articles.body:
A green photograph can start an emerald search, but it should not finish one. Build a brief around the appearance you like and the piece you hope to create. Keep room in that brief for practical questions about the individual stone rather than assuming every emerald will suit the same design.

Start with identity Emerald is a green to bluish-green variety of beryl. Inclusions are an important part of how many emeralds appear. Neither a clean-looking photograph nor visible internal features, by themselves, tell you everything about the identity or condition of a particular example.

Request useful views Ask for an overall face-up view, a side view and a video of the exact item. Note whether the image shows the entire outline. A simple comparison sheet can record your preferred appearance alongside dimensions and the seller's reference number, leaving space for answers you still need.

Discuss enhancement and care Ask what treatment or clarity enhancement has been disclosed for that emerald. Bring the answer to the jeweller who will set or maintain it. Request care instructions for the specific stone and setting rather than copying a general cleaning routine from another piece of jewellery.

Decide with the whole record Before choosing, check that the quotation, photographs and available report all correspond to the same item. Revisit your preferred design and ask whether the proposed setting has been reviewed by the maker. A well-organized purchase leaves you with a stone you enjoy, a workable design conversation and a written record you can keep with the finished piece.

articles.title: Amethyst: Planning a Jewellery Design Around Purple
articles.summary: Use purple amethyst as the starting point for a clear color, shape and jewellery design brief.
articles.body:
Amethyst offers an inviting starting point for a purple jewellery design. Rather than beginning with a long list of stones, think about the finished piece: a pendant, a ring or an earring pair. Decide how much visual presence you want and which existing clothes or jewellery the new piece should work with.

Understand the material Amethyst is the purple variety of quartz. Its identity is separate from the name of its outline: an oval amethyst and a cushion-shaped amethyst can belong to the same gem variety while presenting different design possibilities. Keep material and shape in separate columns when comparing listings.

Make a color brief Collect two or three references for the purple appearance you prefer. Treat them as conversation starters, not promises of an exact match. Ask the seller to identify which actual stones are closest to your brief, and request photographs of those items rather than a representative stock image.

Compare the complete outline Record measurements and sketch the stone at approximate actual size on paper. Place the sketch next to the kind of chain, ring or earrings you plan to wear. This simple exercise turns an enlarged screen image into a more useful design discussion with the maker.

Keep the choice personal and documented Ask for the item's identity description, treatment information and suitable care guidance. Then compare the candidates against your original idea, including the proposed setting cost. The strongest design brief is specific enough to guide the project while leaving space for the jeweller to explain what will work best for the selected stone.

articles.title: Citrine: Building a Warm Yellow Gemstone Shortlist
articles.summary: A practical way to compare citrine candidates and plan a warm-toned gemstone design.
articles.body:
If your design brief begins with warm yellow or orange, citrine is a useful gem to explore. Start by describing the effect you want: a soft accent, a bright focal point or a coordinated pair. This keeps the search centered on your project rather than on whichever listing has the most elaborate description.

Know what citrine means Citrine is a yellow to orange variety of quartz. Its name identifies a gem variety, while terms used to describe a particular shade may be more subjective. Ask the seller to explain unfamiliar descriptions and to provide the treatment information associated with the actual item.

Compare candidates consistently Choose a small group of stones and ask for photographs made in similar conditions. For each candidate, save the reference number, dimensions and asking price. Add one sentence describing what appeals to you. Those personal notes can make a later comparison easier than relying on memory.

Think about the whole piece Bring the shortlist to the jeweller with your preferred metal, design references and intended use. Ask for a proposed setting based on the stone's actual measurements. If you want matching earrings, request a view of the pair together and discuss what degree of matching matters to you.

Finish with a clear record Before ordering, confirm which stone is reserved, what is included in the quotation and which details remain to be agreed. Keep the photographs and written description together. A thoughtful citrine selection is a design decision supported by item-specific information, not a race to find the largest number on a product card.

articles.title: Garnet Is a Family: Asking Better Questions About Your Stone
articles.summary: Learn why the word garnet needs a more specific description when you are comparing individual gemstones.
articles.body:
The word garnet can lead shoppers to imagine one familiar dark red stone. In practice, the name covers a group of related minerals, and garnets appear in a range of colors. That makes a more specific description especially useful when you begin comparing listings for a jewellery project.

Ask which garnet is offered Request the variety or species description used for the actual item. An orange spessartine listing gives you a different starting point from a general garnet label. If the wording is unclear, ask the seller to explain it and identify the information supporting that description.

Write a project-led shortlist Start a comparison table with your preferred color, shape and intended piece. Add actual dimensions, the item reference and the quoted price for each candidate. Keep your visual preferences separate from facts you are still checking, so an appealing image does not silently become an identification claim.

Bring the stone into the design conversation Show the selected candidates to the person who will make the jewellery. Discuss the outline you prefer, the proposed setting and how you plan to use the finished piece. Request item-specific advice about suitability and maintenance rather than assuming every stone carrying the garnet name behaves identically.

Keep the description precise Your final record should identify the selected item clearly and preserve the seller's wording about identity and treatments. Where additional testing or a report is part of the purchase, confirm the scope before ordering it. A precise description gives both buyer and maker a better foundation than a broad family name alone.

articles.title: Spinel: Keeping Identity Separate from Color
articles.summary: Explore spinel through a practical comparison of material identity, color preference and design requirements.
articles.body:
Color is a useful way to begin a gemstone search, but it cannot do all the work. Spinel provides a good example: it occurs in several colors and has its own mineral identity. Start with the appearance you like, then ask what the individual stone is and how that identification has been described.

Begin with the correct name Spinel is a gem material distinct from ruby and sapphire, even when a color invites comparison. Historical naming confusion is a reminder to use the specific identity supplied for the item rather than treating resemblance as proof. Keep the material name visible on your shortlist.

Plan a focused comparison Select a few candidates in the color direction you prefer. Request a full outline view and a side view of each, with the item reference attached. Record dimensions and write down the visual qualities that matter to your design, such as a geometric outline or a strong central accent.

Ask about the individual example Request natural or laboratory-grown disclosure, treatment information and any available independent identification. If a report is offered, make sure it refers to the selected stone. Do not rely on a report photograph that cannot be connected clearly to the item you intend to receive.

Translate the shortlist into a design Discuss the selected stone with the maker before finalizing a setting. Share the intended use, preferred metal and your visual references. A useful spinel purchase combines a material you understand with an appearance you enjoy and a design plan that has been checked against the actual stone.

articles.title: Bi-Color Tourmaline: Designing Around More Than One Color
articles.summary: Turn a bi-color tourmaline's color arrangement into a clear, practical jewellery design brief.
articles.body:
A gemstone with more than one visible color asks for a slightly different design conversation. Instead of choosing a single shade, you are choosing an arrangement: where each color appears and how the outline presents the combination. Begin with that arrangement when exploring bi-color tourmaline.

Understand the visual feature Tourmaline can show different color zones within the same crystal. Some cut stones display a visible combination of colors, including pink and green. The exact arrangement belongs to the individual stone, so a representative photograph cannot show you how every bi-color example will look.

Request the exact item Ask for photographs of the stone being offered, including its complete outline. Mark which end or side you would like at the top of the finished design. This gives the jeweller a specific orientation to discuss instead of leaving a major visual choice unspoken.

Compare composition rather than labels Place shortlisted images side by side and note the distribution you prefer. Record the measurements and item numbers. If two stones both use the same trade description, keep comparing their actual appearance; matching words do not make them interchangeable for your project.

Agree on the design direction Bring the stone's photographs and measurements to the maker. Discuss how the setting will frame the colors and whether your preferred orientation has practical constraints. Confirm identity, treatment disclosure and the selected item in writing. A well-planned bi-color design begins with the individual stone's composition and carries that idea through to the finished piece.

articles.title: Quartz Jewellery: Comparing Purple, Yellow and Colorless Designs
articles.summary: Build a quartz design shortlist by separating variety names, visual preferences and the requirements of the finished piece.
articles.body:
Quartz can appear in very different jewellery conversations. Purple amethyst and yellow-to-orange citrine are familiar quartz varieties, yet they suggest different design directions. When comparing stones, separate the family name from the variety, color description and shape. Each answers a different question about what you are looking at.

Define the role of the stone Decide whether the gem should provide the main color, support another stone or create a restrained focal point. Write a one-sentence design brief before browsing. This can be as simple as a purple pendant for an existing chain or a warm yellow accent for a new ring.

Compare actual candidates Ask for the variety name used for each item, its measurements and the exact reference number. Request photographs of the stones being offered. Record your personal response to each candidate without turning that response into a claim about identity, treatment or origin.

Make room for the setting Show the shortlist to the maker with the preferred metal and intended use. Ask how the actual outline and depth will influence the proposed design. If the stone must fit an existing mount, share the mount's measurements and have compatibility checked before purchasing.

Keep the information together Save the seller's identity description, treatment disclosure, care guidance and final quotation in the same folder as the photographs. A quartz design does not need a complicated buying process. It needs a clear project, a specific stone and enough written information for you and the jeweller to discuss the same item confidently.

articles.title: Gemstone Shapes Explained: Outline and Faceting Are Different Choices
articles.summary: Separate a gemstone's outline from its faceting style so you can describe the design you actually want.
articles.body:
Round, oval, pear and cushion describe outlines that are easy to recognize. Brilliant and step-cut describe aspects of how facets are arranged. Treating shape and faceting as separate parts of your brief makes it easier to explain a design and compare candidates without relying on a single broad label.

Start with the silhouette Choose the outline that best suits your project. A long silhouette and a compact square create different visual starting points, even before you compare the material. Draw a few simple outlines on paper and note which proportions feel right for the intended piece.

Look inside the outline Faceting arrangements influence the pattern of reflections you see. When reviewing candidates, ask for images that show the whole stone and request a short video. Write down the visual effect you enjoy rather than assuming every stone sharing one outline will look the same.

Read the dimensions Record length, width and depth, not just the shape name. An oval description does not tell the jeweller exactly how elongated the item is. If an existing setting is involved, have the maker assess fit using the selected stone's actual measurements.

Create a usable brief Your final note can combine material, outline, preferred proportions, visual references and intended use. Ask the cutter or jeweller to explain any practical trade-offs for the actual stone. This turns a list of attractive shapes into a design discussion with clear priorities and room for informed advice.

articles.title: Gemstone Color: Describing What You See More Clearly
articles.summary: Use hue, tone and saturation to make gemstone color preferences easier to discuss and compare.
articles.body:
Two people can both ask for a blue stone and imagine quite different results. More precise color language helps narrow that gap. You do not need to become a professional grader to give a seller or jeweller a clearer account of what you like.

Separate three color questions Hue identifies the color family. Tone describes relative lightness or darkness, while saturation concerns the strength of the color. Use these as conversation tools: a preference for a lighter blue says something different from a preference for a more intense blue.

Write a simple preference note Collect a small number of visual references and describe each in your own words. Ask which real candidates are closest to that direction. Keep the references separate from the product photographs so there is no confusion about which image represents an actual item for sale.

Compare with a consistent process Request comparable views of your shortlisted stones and note the conditions described by the seller. Look at the same candidates together before adding more options. If a listing uses a poetic or unfamiliar color term, ask for a plain-language explanation.

Connect color to the finished piece Share the shortlist with the maker alongside your preferred metal and design references. Explain which color quality you most want to preserve in the overall look. A clear color brief helps everyone work toward the same visual goal while keeping identity, treatment information and origin claims as separate questions to verify.

articles.title: Carat Weight and Gemstone Size: Read Both Before You Choose
articles.summary: Learn what a carat measures and build a shortlist that includes the dimensions your jewellery project needs.
articles.body:
A carat number is useful, but it does not describe a complete gemstone. When planning jewellery, keep the weight and measurements together. One tells you how much the stone weighs; the other helps you and the maker discuss its physical fit and the visual proportions you want.

Know the unit One metric carat equals 0.2 grams. Carat weight is therefore a measurement of mass, not a direct measurement of width or length. Keep it distinct from karat terminology used for gold purity, especially when reading a listing that describes both a stone and its proposed metal.

Add the measurements For every candidate, record length, width and depth in millimeters. Ask whether the listed weight describes the loose stone or another quantity, such as the combined weight of several stones. A clear answer prevents a small number on a listing from being interpreted incorrectly.

Test your design expectations Sketch the outline at approximately the listed dimensions. Bring that sketch, the measurements and the intended design to the maker. If you are adapting an existing mount, request a fit assessment before selecting the stone rather than trying to solve a mismatch afterward.

Compare the whole candidate Use weight as one column in your shortlist alongside appearance, dimensions, identity information and quoted cost. Do not let a target weight erase the qualities that originally attracted you to the design. The goal is a stone that suits the project and a record that makes its specifications easy to understand.

articles.title: Gemstone Origins: What a Country Name Can and Cannot Tell You
articles.summary: Keep geographic origin, the seller's location and the identity of the individual gemstone separate when reviewing a listing.
articles.body:
An origin name can make a gemstone story memorable, but the story still needs a clear connection to the individual stone. Before comparing country labels, separate three questions: what material is offered, what geographic origin is claimed and what information supports that claim.

Ask what the location describes A seller's address, a cutting location and a gemstone's geographic origin are different kinds of information. Request plain wording about which one is being described. A broad regional label can also be less specific than a country claim, so keep the original description in your notes.

Understand the scope of an opinion Gemological origin determination involves interpreting evidence and comparing it with reference information. It is not available or conclusive for every stone. Ask whether an offered report includes an origin opinion and read its actual conclusion rather than assuming every identification report covers geography.

Keep the item connection intact Save the stone's reference number with its photographs and any report details. Ask the seller to explain how those records correspond to the item you will receive. If one document uses different wording from the listing, request clarification before treating the two descriptions as equivalent.

Make room for appearance and purpose Record what you enjoy about the stone separately from its origin description. Discuss the design with the maker using the actual measurements. A country name can be part of a well-documented purchase, but it should not replace your assessment of the selected item or the project you want it to serve.

articles.title: How to Read a Colored Gemstone Laboratory Report
articles.summary: A straightforward checklist for connecting a laboratory report to the gemstone you are considering.
articles.body:
A laboratory report is most useful when you know which questions it addresses. Begin with the specific stone you are considering and the information you want confirmed. Then read the document as a record of findings, keeping its scope separate from the seller's marketing description.

Check the service described GIA's colored stone services can address identity, natural or laboratory-grown status and detectable treatments. Some report services also offer geographic origin opinions for eligible materials. Read the report type and actual results rather than assuming every document includes the same investigations.

Match the report to the item Compare the identifying information supplied with the report against the seller's listing. Review measurements, weight where applicable, description and reference details. Ask the seller to resolve inconsistencies and explain how the report is connected to the item you intend to receive.

Preserve the exact wording Record the laboratory's name, report number and the findings relevant to your decision. If the laboratory offers an official verification service, use that official route. A seller's uploaded image or a logo on a page is not a replacement for reading and checking the actual document.

Keep other decisions separate Use the report alongside your visual comparison, design requirements and the written commercial terms. Ask separately for any appraisal or price opinion you require; do not assume it is included in the report you have been shown. The best reading habit is simple: establish what the document covers, connect it to the stone and keep unanswered questions visible.

articles.title: Gemstone Treatments: Questions Worth Asking Before You Buy
articles.summary: Turn an unfamiliar treatment description into a focused conversation about the actual gemstone and its maintenance.
articles.body:
Treatment information belongs beside a gemstone's identity, measurements and item reference. Ask for it early in the comparison process so you can discuss the selected stone with the jeweller who may set or maintain it. A clear written answer is more useful than an unexplained label.

Know why the question matters Gem treatments can affect appearance or other characteristics. Examples discussed by gemological laboratories include heating, filling and diffusion processes. The relevant treatment, if any, depends on the actual material and item. A general statement about a gem family does not establish the history of one stone.

Request precise wording Ask what treatment has been disclosed, who supplied that information and whether it is addressed by an available laboratory report. Keep the original wording in your shortlist. If a listing simply says enhanced, request an explanation rather than filling the gap with an assumption.

Bring the answer to the maker Share the treatment statement before the stone is set, repaired or cleaned. Ask for a maintenance plan appropriate to that item and the proposed setting. This keeps the design conversation connected to the information you actually have instead of relying on a generic routine.

Make the decision with the disclosure included Compare candidates with their treatment descriptions visible, alongside appearance, dimensions and quotation. Ask the seller to clarify any difference between a listing and a report. You do not need to memorize every process to shop more carefully; you need to request clear disclosure and preserve it with the record of the selected gemstone.

articles.title: Natural, Laboratory-Grown and Imitation Gems: Clearer Buying Language
articles.summary: Understand three different descriptions so you can request the material that fits your expectations.
articles.body:
Before choosing a gemstone, make sure the material description matches your expectations. Natural, laboratory-grown and imitation are not interchangeable terms. A clear conversation about identity gives your design brief a firmer starting point and helps prevent a color resemblance from being mistaken for a material identification.

Separate formation from resemblance A laboratory-grown counterpart has essentially the same chemical composition, crystal structure and relevant properties as its natural counterpart, but is made through a controlled growth process. An imitation is selected to resemble another gem and can be a different material. These descriptions answer different questions about what the item is.

Ask for the full description Request the material name and whether it is described as natural, laboratory-grown, assembled or an imitation. Avoid relying on words such as genuine or real without clarification. Ask the seller to put the specific identity description in the written record for the item you choose.

Keep treatment as another question Identity and treatment history should each have a place on your comparison sheet. Request the available information for the actual stone rather than treating one answer as automatically resolving the other. Discuss any uncertainty before committing to a design or purchase.

Connect the language to your project Explain your preferences to the jeweller in practical terms: the material category you want, the appearance you enjoy and the intended piece. Where independent identification forms part of your decision, agree on that step before ordering. Clear terminology helps the finished project reflect the choice you intended to make.

articles.title: A Simple Gemstone Care Record for Your Jewellery
articles.summary: Create a useful care record that follows the individual gemstone, its treatments and its setting.
articles.body:
The most useful care guide is one you can connect to the jewellery you actually own. Instead of collecting unrelated cleaning tips, create a short record for each piece. Keep it with the purchase information so anyone who later maintains the jewellery can begin with the same facts.

Record the identity and disclosures Write down the material description, disclosed treatments, item reference and any laboratory report details. GIA notes that treatment information is relevant to care, and that heat and light can affect some gem materials. Share the available information when asking a professional for instructions.

Request a piece-specific routine Ask the jeweller how to clean and store the finished item, and whether any methods should be avoided for that stone and setting. Do not assume that a routine suitable for another piece will also suit this one. Keep the response in the same care record rather than depending on memory.

Make maintenance easy to follow Add the maker's contact details, the date of any inspection and the work performed. If a setting is repaired or a stone is replaced, update the record. A short, accurate note can be more useful than a long document that no longer describes the piece.

Pass the record along When jewellery is given as a gift, include its care information with the presentation. Tell the recipient where the documents are stored and which professional has worked on the piece. A good routine begins with knowing what you own and knowing where to ask when the next maintenance question appears.

A gemstone choice becomes more practical when it begins with the finished piece. A ring, pendant and pair of earrings create different design conversations. Discuss suitability with the maker Gemstone durability involves more than scratch resistance; toughness and stability also matter. Bring the selected material and any treatment information to the jeweller. Ask for advice about its suitability for the intended use and proposed setting rather than assuming a single hardness number settles the decision.

Define the design requirements For a ring, describe the profile and overall style you prefer. For a pendant, discuss the orientation, chain and proportions. For earrings, explain whether you want a close match or a deliberately varied pair. These are useful project questions even before a stone has been selected.

Use actual measurements Give the maker the dimensions of the shortlisted items and request a design response based on those stones. If an existing mount is part of the project, ask for compatibility to be assessed before purchasing. Keep the stone selection and setting proposal connected throughout the conversation.

Confirm the complete brief Save the agreed item references, metal choice, setting design, care guidance and quotation together. Note any decisions that are still open. A successful project is easier to coordinate when the buyer and maker share one clear record of the stone, the design and the intended use.

articles.title: Your First Loose Gemstone: A Practical Shortlisting Method
articles.summary: A manageable, project-led workflow for comparing a first loose gemstone without losing track of important information.
articles.body:
Buying a first loose gemstone can feel like comparing too many things at once. A simple shortlist reduces that confusion. Begin with a project rather than a product feed: the piece you want to create, the visual direction you enjoy and the information you want in hand before deciding.

Write a one-page brief Choose a color direction, a few preferred shapes and the intended use. Add a spending limit that leaves room for any setting work you plan. Use gemological reference material to learn unfamiliar names, while keeping your design priorities separate from general descriptions of a gem variety.

Limit the first comparison Ask for three suitable candidates. Give each its own row with an item reference, actual dimensions, asking price and links to the supplied images. Add a short personal note about what you like. This creates a manageable comparison before you consider requesting additional options.

List the unanswered questions Ask for the material identity, treatment disclosure and available documentation for the actual items. Keep uncertainties visible instead of replacing them with assumptions. Share the shortlist with the maker if the gemstone will become a piece of jewellery, and ask for a practical design assessment.

Close the loop before ordering Confirm the selected item, the written description and the commercial terms directly with the seller. Save the agreed information with the quotation. A first purchase does not need to be a perfect lesson in every aspect of gemology; it needs a clear process that connects your preferences to a specific, adequately described stone.

articles.title: Gemstone Photographs: What to Request Before Choosing Online
articles.summary: Build an image request that shows the actual gemstone clearly and keeps illustrative images separate from inventory photographs.
articles.body:
An online gemstone photograph should help you ask informed questions about a specific item. Start by checking whether you are viewing that item or an illustration. Attractive imagery is useful for exploring a design direction, but the final comparison should be connected to the stone being offered.

Request a useful image set Ask for an overall face-up view, an outline view and a side view, with the same item reference attached to each. A short video can be another useful part of the comparison. Tell the seller which visual questions you want the images to answer rather than simply asking for more pictures.

Ask about the presentation Lighting, background and color balance are relevant parts of gemstone photography. GIA's photography guidance discusses controlling the presentation and recording how a gem really looks. Ask for an explanation when two images of the same candidate appear noticeably different.

Keep references clearly labeled Store design inspiration separately from actual inventory photographs. AI-generated imagery should be identified as illustrative and should not be presented as documentary evidence of a particular stone's color, inclusions, origin or condition. When sharing a brief with the maker, label each image by its purpose.

Keep the documents in the comparison Save the image set alongside measurements, identity information and any available report. If you are still uncertain about the appearance, request clarification before making a decision.
